# Packaging and deployment {#sec-shipping}

An app that only runs on your machine is not done. This chapter turns a build into something
a user can download, with everything it needs to run and every license it has to include.

## Install, then deploy {#sec-deploy}

Shipping starts with two steps. `install()` copies your app into a clean folder. Qt's deploy
script then copies everything your app needs from Qt next to it: libraries, plugins and QML
modules.

```{.cmake filename="src/app/CMakeLists.txt"}
install(TARGETS app
    BUNDLE DESTINATION .
    RUNTIME DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR}
)
qt_generate_deploy_qml_app_script(TARGET app OUTPUT_SCRIPT deploy_script)
install(SCRIPT ${deploy_script})
```

```sh
cmake --install build/release --prefix dist
```

`dist/` now runs on a machine without Qt: a self-contained `.app` bundle on macOS, a folder
with the executable and its DLLs on Windows, a `bin/` and `lib/` tree on Linux.

::: {.callout-warning}
## "Could not find or load the Qt platform plugin"
The most famous Qt error means the deploy step did not run, or ran without the plugins.
Qt loads plugins at run time, so a build that starts on your machine can still fail on
another one.
:::

On Windows, the deploy script knows Qt's DLLs but not those of your other dependencies.
Install them too, with `install(FILES $<TARGET_RUNTIME_DLLS:app> ...)`.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/app/CMakeLists.txt`

**Read more:** [Deploying Qt applications with CMake](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/cmake-deployment.html)
:::

## One package per platform {#sec-packages}

CPack, part of CMake, turns the installed app into the format each platform expects:

| Platform | Format | CPack generator |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | disk image (`.dmg`) | `DragNDrop` |
| Windows | archive or installer | `ZIP`, `NSIS`, `WIX` |
| Linux | archive or package | `TGZ`, `DEB`, `RPM` |

```{.cmake filename="cmake/Packaging.cmake"}
set(CPACK_PACKAGE_FILE_NAME
    "${PROJECT_NAME}-${PROJECT_VERSION}-${CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME}")
if(APPLE)
    set(CPACK_GENERATOR DragNDrop)
elseif(WIN32)
    set(CPACK_GENERATOR ZIP)
else()
    set(CPACK_GENERATOR TGZ)
endif()
include(CPack)
```

With a package preset, `cmake --workflow --preset release` configures, builds, tests and
packages in one go. Before you hand the package to users, sign it (@sec-distribution).

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/Packaging.cmake`

**Read more:** [CPack](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CPack.html)
:::

## Licenses are part of the product {#sec-licenses}

Every library and asset you ship comes with a license, and most licenses ask for something
in return.

**Qt** is available under the LGPLv3 (and a commercial license). For an app you distribute,
the LGPL asks you to:

- let users replace Qt with their own build; linking Qt dynamically is the simple way;
- ship Qt's license texts and say that your app uses Qt;
- provide Qt's source code, or a written offer for it;
- avoid the Qt modules that are available only under the GPL.

**Every other dependency and asset** needs its license shipped as well: libraries, but also
fonts and icons. Put one text file per component into a `licenses/` folder of the package.
Install that folder in the platform's package-data location, then let people open it from the
About dialog.

**Your own repository** should say clearly what is yours and under which terms. The
[REUSE](https://reuse.software/) convention does that in one file:

```{.toml filename="REUSE.toml"}
version = 1

[[annotations]]
path = "**"
SPDX-FileCopyrightText = "2026 Your Name"
SPDX-License-Identifier = "MIT-0"

[[annotations]]
path = "src/controls/fonts/**"
SPDX-FileCopyrightText = "2016 The Inter Project Authors"
SPDX-License-Identifier = "OFL-1.1"
```

`reuse lint` then checks that every file in the repository is covered.

This is a summary of obligations, not legal advice.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `REUSE.toml`, `app_add_notice()` in `cmake/Packaging.cmake`, and the About dialog

**Read more:** [Qt licensing](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/licensing.html)
:::

## CI builds what you ship {#sec-ci}

Every change should build, test and package on every platform you support, on a machine that
is not yours. Use the same preset command that developers run:

```{.yaml filename=".github/workflows/ci.yml"}
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-24.04, macos-15, windows-2022]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          submodules: true
      - uses: jurplel/install-qt-action@v4
        with:
          version: "6.12.0"
          cache: true
      - run: cmake --workflow --preset release
```

A complete workflow also sets up the compiler environment on Windows. Cache the dependency
builds between runs (vcpkg's binary cache does this), or every run rebuilds them from
scratch. Upload the packages as build artifacts, so every change produces
something you can download and try.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Package for an empty machine

Before shipping, picture a machine with none of your development environment: no installed
fonts, libraries, tools, or configuration. Package every required runtime component, then test
the result on such a machine.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
:::

## Versions, releases and backports {#sec-versions-and-backports}

A **version** tells a user which release they have. With
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html), a version has three numbers:

| Change | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Patch | `1.2.0` → `1.2.1` | a backward-compatible bug fix |
| Minor | `1.2.1` → `1.3.0` | backward-compatible functionality |
| Major | `1.3.0` → `2.0.0` | an incompatible public change |

These promises need a defined public contract: for an app that might include a file format,
an API or commands used by scripts. Before `1.0.0`, SemVer treats the public API as unstable.
A **tag** such as `v1.2.0` names the exact commit used for a release; a branch can continue
moving as more fixes are added.

Now imagine users run both version `1.2` and the newer `2.2`. You discover a serious bug in
both. Fix and test it on `main` for the next release, then bring the same fix to the
`release/1.2` maintenance branch. That branch starts at the old release and contains only
the fixes the team chooses to support there. Test the backport and release `1.2.1`, tagged
at its own commit. Users can receive the fix without upgrading to version 2.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A["v1.2.0<br/>released"] --> B["v2.2.0<br/>released"] --> C["Fix on main"]
    A --> D["release/1.2<br/>maintenance"] --> E["Backport fix<br/>tag v1.2.1"]
    C -. "copy the fix" .-> E
```

Copying a commit to another branch is called **cherry-picking** or **backporting**. An atomic
fix is easier to pick because it brings the fix and its test without unrelated features:

```sh
git switch release/1.2
git cherry-pick -x <fix-commit>
```

The result is a new commit on the maintenance branch. The `-x` option records the original
commit when the pick applies without conflicts; after resolving a conflict, check the message
and add that reference if needed. A fix may need adaptation if version 1 has different code.
Maintain older branches only for releases you have chosen to support.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakeLists.txt` sets the app version; the release build puts it in the package

**Read more:** [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html),
[Git tags](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging),
[Git cherry-pick](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-cherry-pick)
:::
